The Wordmark
Gate

Every poster was coming out with the same wordmark, and the rule meant to keep it legible was quietly enforcing that. Fifty test images judged by eye first and measured afterwards — and the only real boundary turned out to be the one Marcus stated in a sentence.

Reviewed by the band

The band has now seen this work. Reported 2026‑08‑30: every member read the shared material and looked at the artwork. They like the wordmark, the skull, the year rings and the timeline, and they love the illustrated generated work.

That is a response to a direction, not a signature on each item. Individual artefacts, whether Böbbis becomes a standing per-release character, whether the skull is ever publicly named, and printing or selling anything are all still open. Where a direction was chosen inside a round, that was Marcus’s call.

Start with the plain-language overview if you haven’t already.

1

Where this sits

Every illustrated poster ends the same way: the real APEZONE wordmark is laid across the top of the picture. The letterforms never change — they always come from the shipped master file. What changes is the colour and the surface treatment: whether the letters are flat, embossed, banded, gradient, outlined.

This round is about how that choice gets made. It is not a design round and it produced no new artwork. It fixed a machine that had quietly started giving the same answer every time, and then fixed the rule that was stopping it giving different ones.

It ran on zero image generations and cost nothing in credits.

2

Not artwork

Nothing on this page is a finished cover or poster. The pictures here are the pipeline's test images — explorations from the Böbbis character rounds, reused because they are the kind of picture the wordmark has to sit on. They are shown to demonstrate a measurement, not to propose a design.

The band has reviewed and accepted the current illustrated work. Open decision 12 — the generation licence — still gates print and merchandise; that production limit is separate from creative approval.

3

The complaint: every poster came out the same

Marcus, looking at a run of finished posters: “It seems now every generation creates a similar wordmark style each time. Have we strangled the process on it?” And then, more precisely: “I already earlier requested we always create the style based on the image we generate and see what type of wordmark style fits the image the best. Now it seems to drive on the chisel each and every time. And it's boring.”

He was right. Here are five of the eight available treatments on the same picture, as the pipeline was then producing them.

4

Why: a score can only ever give one answer

The cause was not a bad default. It was that two separate decisions had been handed to a measurement — and the measurement in question scores contrast. Ask for the highest-contrast option and you get the most contrasty one, on every picture, forever.

Which treatment. One treatment, chisel, measured highest on six pictures out of six. Not because it suited them — because it is simply the most contrasty of the eight. On the Kauppatori gull poster it is also the palest, washing the burnt orange out to salmon. It wins the measurement and loses the picture.

Which colour. Earlier the same day the colour derivation had been switched to a different method because it scored higher on the gates — the identical mistake, one layer down. That method takes the brightest highlight in the picture, which is near-white almost anywhere, so every mark came out the same cream:

PictureOld methodSaturationNew methodSaturation
Kauppatori#F5E7C80.18#CF633C0.71
Senate Square#A3958A0.15#1B88FF0.89
Rodeo#C29F750.40#A3744F0.52
Cassette#ECE2C40.17#5C938C0.37

Saturation is how much colour a shade has, from 0 (grey) to 1 (vivid). The old method was returning near-greys; the replacement reads a colour out of the picture's own palette.

That replacement was itself wrong, and Marcus found it the next day. He looked at eight treatments of the worship poster, every one of them blue, and said he would have taken a neon from the beam instead. He was right, and it was still a bug rather than a matter of taste.

The palette that replacement chooses from is built by area, so it merges away small saturated flats — on that picture it contains no saturated colour at all. The scorer therefore picked #040C1E: chroma 26, luminance 0.004. That is black. It only measured as “saturated” because the ratio it uses is large for a near-black pixel. The colour was then brightened until it was legible, and out came #417BFF, chroma 189. The blue was never in the picture — it was manufactured out of black.

Meanwhile 7.7% of that picture's pixels carry strong colour, 35% of it cyan. All of it invisible to the palette. See §13.

The project already had the correct rule written down — the gate vetoes rather than chooses — which is exactly why an earlier wave of posters had shipped eleven different treatments between them.

5

What changed: the treatment is named, not measured

The surface treatment is now a design decision written into each poster's own file by a person. The gate can refuse it, and if it does the build stops and prints every option with its score — but it never silently substitutes a different one.

Three posters were rebuilt. Three different treatments, three different colours:

PosterTreatmentWordmark colour
Kauppatori gulltriband#CF633C burnt orange
Senate Square UFOdeepblock#1B7DFF electric blue
Humanoid worshipemboss#427EFF cosmic blue
6

Freedom: the eight are not a ceiling

Marcus: “I rather have no rule to create a certain wordmark style, but a style created based on what suits the image the best. As otherwise every image wordmark starts repeating itself if we lock it to just certain styles.”

The colour can be named per poster as well, which closed an asymmetry this round originally left standing: the treatment became a design decision made by a person while the colour was still made entirely by the machine. Both are now nameable, and the gate vetoes either.

A poster can now define its own treatment and hand it to the pipeline — a ninth, a tenth, one that exists for a single cover and never again. It clears exactly the same gate as the built-in eight; there is no exemption for being bespoke. The Rodeo single cover already worked this way for its title, building a perspective-mapped lamp matrix out of colours taken from the picture.

One boundary held deliberately: written in code, yes — generated by a model, no. This has been tested. Wordmark round three pointed an image generator at the mark and asked it for surface treatments. All ten candidates came back a different word. A model asked to relight type will happily redraw it, and the result looks better while no longer being our name.

Neither of the gates on this page can detect that — they measure whether a mark separates from its background, not whether it still says APEZONE. A script that repaints the master's outlines cannot make that mistake; a generator makes it by default.

7

The defect Marcus found in the boundary

He asked for one hard rule to keep the freedom safe: “we need some hard boundaries of course so it does not create a dark one for example on a dark background.” Then corrected himself a minute later:

Marcus, a minute later

“But it can even be a dark one on dark background if it has a light stroke.” 😛

That correction found a real bug. The existing gate refused that mark.

The reason is that the old gate's first question was “is the outer band of the mark dark?” — a stand-in for “will it contrast with the artwork” that let it avoid ever looking at the artwork. A near-black outline works on almost any picture, so the shortcut was reasonable. Its cost was never written down: it made one polarity compulsory. Light letters with a dark outline, always. Marcus's inverse could not pass, no matter how well it read.

8

Calibrating against the eye, in that order

The obvious move — adjust the gate until it accepts the mark — is exactly the trap. The original measurement carries its own warning that it had been rewritten twice and must not be fitted to a hoped-for result, and by this point it had been rewritten twice more in a single session, each time to admit something it had just refused.

So the order was forced by the files themselves:

  1. Build the corpus with no numbers in it. Ten treatments × five background pictures spanning very dark to near-white = 50 composites, saved as plain contact sheets carrying nothing but a label.
  2. Judge them by eye and write the verdicts to a file — reads, marginal or fails — before computing anything.
  3. Only then measure, and see which rule separates the verdicts.

The result was lopsided in a way that matters:

VerdictCountWhich
reads42the great majority
marginal4horizon and duograd on the two dark pictures
fails4darkflat on the two dark pictures; lightflat on the two light ones

The four outright failures are a flat mark, no outline, whose brightness matches its background. Nothing else in fifty fails. The boundary Marcus asked for turned out to be the only real one there is.

9

The gate became one question

Two of the three conditions were dropped, and not for tidiness:

  • Letterform-against-its-own-outline reads 1.00 for all four failures — and for a flat black mark on teal that reads perfectly well. A flat mark has no outline, so the question is meaningless and it separates nothing.
  • The enclosure check returned 1.000 on all fifty cells. It was recovering its own boundary and measuring geometry rather than ink. A check that returns the same number for every input is not a weak check — it is not a check.

What remained is one question, asked about the picture rather than about the mark:

Does the mark separate from the artwork actually underneath it — by either its letterforms or its outline, whichever is doing the work?

Nothing about light or dark appears in it, so polarity is free by construction. Light letters on a dark ground pass on the letterform. Marcus's dark letters with a light stroke pass on the outline. A flat mark matching its background has neither, and fails.

10

Marcus again: the average was hiding it

That version agreed with the eye on the 42-and-4 split, but it could not see the four marginal cases — they scored far above the passing threshold. Marcus named the mechanism without seeing any of the numbers:

Marcus, on the first calibrated version

“Horizon and duograd gets a little too dark on the dark end… on a dark background.”

Both are gradient treatments. The dark end of the gradient lands on dark artwork and the mark dies in a band, while the rest of the letterform carries the average up.

So the gate now asks its one question six times down the letterform and takes the worst slice. On the same fifty verdicts — not re-judged, only with marginal counted as a negative, which is what his observation says it should be:

Scored howLowest that readsHighest that doesn'tVerdict
Whole mark1.915.67overlaps — no separation at all
Worst of six slices1.581.32separates — agrees with the eye 50/50

Six slices is not a tuned number. Three, four and six all separate cleanly — a threshold that works across a contiguous range is not balanced on one lucky value. Eight and twelve break, for a reason that can be checked: a slice lands inside a thin horizontal stroke and the measurement goes to noise, collapsing a mark that reads perfectly well. Six is the finest count before that starts.

A rejection now names the slice that died, so the build says where the mark fails rather than only that it did.

11

What the old rule had been costing

Scored on the same fifty composites, at the size the pipeline actually uses:

Agrees with the eyeRejects marks that readPasses marks that fail
Old pair of gates30 / 50200
New gate50 / 5000

Every one of the old rule's twenty disagreements is a rejection of something that reads. It never let a bad mark through — it was not wrong about danger, it was wildly over-cautious, and what it rejected was precisely the interesting half: every dark-letters-with-a-light-stroke mark on every ground, and both flat marks wherever they legitimately work.

Across the three posters that have been built through the pipeline, the set of treatments allowed to carry a poster goes from 18 of 24 to 24 of 24 — and then correctly narrows again on the two dark pictures once the slicing lands, dropping duograd and horizon there while keeping them on the mid-toned Kauppatori picture where they read.

12

What this round concluded

  • A legibility score cannot answer a design question. It was answering two, and both collapsed to a single repeated result. The treatment is now named per poster; the gate only vetoes.
  • The wordmark's colour comes from the picture's palette, not its brightest highlight — the difference between saturation 0.15–0.40 and 0.37–0.89.
  • A poster may invent its own treatment. Written in code, gated identically. Generated by a model, never — on measured evidence.
  • The only real boundary is the one Marcus stated: a flat mark whose brightness matches its background. Everything else in a fifty-cell corpus reads.
  • The gate asks about the artwork, six times down the letterform, and knows nothing about light or dark.
13

Corrected along the way

Four things on the record were wrong and are now superseded. They are listed because two of them were this session's own work, made hours earlier:

What said itWhat it saidWhat replaced it
build_posterPick the highest-scoring of eight treatmentsNamed per poster; the gate vetoes only
build_poster, same dayTake colour from the brightest highlight, because it scores betterTake it from the picture's palette — the score was the wrong target twice
art-direction.md §5.4“one of eight surface treatments is chosen by measurement”Rewritten: named by a person, vetoed by measurement
keyline.checkThe mark's outer band must be darkDemoted to a reported diagnostic. Still printed, no longer deciding
This page, §4–5The colour fix was to read the picture's paletteSuperseded the next day. That palette is built by area and drops small saturated flats, so the scorer picked a near-black and brightened it into a colour that was never in the picture. Colour now comes from visibly-coloured pixels, and can be named
The whole roundTreatment named by a person, colour derived by the machineBoth nameable. The asymmetry was not defensible once the derivation was shown to be wrong

One older claim was tested and did not reproduce. The notes on the drawn treatment library state that one mark, 08-double-stencil, has nothing holding its letterforms on a light artwork. Put on five backgrounds including two near-white ones, it read clearly on all five. That claim was reasoned from numbers and never checked by looking. It is not being called wrong — a paler, flatter ground than any tested here might still defeat it — but it did not hold on the pictures this project actually makes.

14

Method, and what this cannot show

The fifty verdicts were judged by Claude, not by a person. One observer, one pass, on a screen. The gate is therefore calibrated to a machine's reading of legibility, and nobody in the band has looked at the corpus. That is the largest single caveat on this page and it is not a small one.

  • The test images were rebuilt afterwards, and not re-judged. The E correction of 2026-08-31 regenerated all fifty composites. Rather than ask someone to judge them again, agreement was re-checked and is identical — 50 out of 50, on the same margins. That is sound for a change this small, and it would not be for a change to how a treatment looks. The rule is written into the corpus builder.
  • Four failures is a thin basis. The gap between passing and failing is clean and all four fail by the same mechanism, but a corpus containing more ways to fail would test the threshold harder than one that mostly contains marks that work.
  • The slicing is vertical only. Backgrounds vary sideways too, and a mark that died over a single bright object mid-line would still pass. The observed failure was vertical, so that is what was built.
  • The gate cannot tell whether the mark still says APEZONE. It measures separation and nothing else. That is why a generated treatment stays inadmissible.
  • Nothing here was seen on paper. Screen only, no print proof, no test at thumbnail sizes on a phone, and no check of how any of it survives compression on a streaming platform's cover art.
  • Zero image generations, no credits spent. Every picture used was already in the project.
  • Band review has happened, but the figures on this page remain calibration evidence rather than separate artwork proposals.
